```{r initialization, include=FALSE}

# 'not in' function
'%!in%' <- function(x,y)!('%in%'(x,y))

### Load Libraries ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------
library(readxl)
library(tibble)
library(hextri)
library(beeswarm)
library(ggbeeswarm)
library(waffle)
library(tidyverse)

### Load Data --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Miscellaneous Data -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

## County FIPS code to name crosswalk
county_fips_xwalk <- read.csv("Data/ohio_county_fips_crosswalk.csv") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    fips = stringr::str_pad(fips, width = 3, side = "left", pad = "0"),
    county = paste0(county, " County"))

# actual 2020 election results
results <- readxl::read_xlsx("Data/ohio_2020_congressional_election_results_by_district.xlsx")

# actual 2020 state-wide presidential election results
presidential_results <- data.frame(
  Party = c("Republican", "Democrat", "Libertarian", "Green", "Write-Ins"),
  Votes = c(3154834, 2679165, 67569, 18812, 1822)
  )

  "Data/DECENNIALSF12010.P9.csv",
  colClasses = "character"
)

)

## Demographic Data (2010) - 115th Congressional Districts

  "Data/DECENNIALCD1152010.P9.csv"
)

## Demographic Output Data
# file path to the folder containing the data
data_folder_path <- "Tracts 2010 (alg2)/99_Export Data/Districts by Race v2"
# list all the files within the folder
data_folder_list <- list.files(data_folder_path, full.names = TRUE) %>%
  sort()
# load all files into a single object
race_data <- lapply(data_folder_list, read.csv)
```

```{r format_data, include=FALSE}

### Demographic Data (2010) - Tracts ---------------------------------------------------------------

population_data <- population_data %>%
  dplyr::mutate(`Label..Grouping.` = trimws(`Label..Grouping.`, which = "both",
                                            whitespace = "[ \\t\\r\\n\\h]")) %>%
  dplyr::filter(`Label..Grouping.` %in% c(
    "Total:",
    "Hispanic or Latino",
    "White alone",
    "Black or African American alone",
    "American Indian and Alaska Native alone",
    "Asian alone",
    "Native Hawaiian and Other Pacific Islander alone",
    "Some Other Race alone",
    "Two or More Races:"
  )) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(Race = dplyr::case_match(
    `Label..Grouping.`,
    "Total:" ~ "Population",
    "Hispanic or Latino" ~ "Hispanic",
    "White alone" ~ "White",
    "Black or African American alone" ~ "Black",
    "American Indian and Alaska Native alone" ~ "AIAN",
    "Asian alone" ~ "Asian",
    "Native Hawaiian and Other Pacific Islander alone" ~ "NHPI",
    "Some Other Race alone" ~ "Other",
    "Two or More Races:" ~ "Two or More Races"
  ), .before = 1) %>%
  dplyr::select(-`Label..Grouping.`) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(2:2953, names_to = "Tract", values_to = "Population") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    # total populations for these tracts have additional alphanumeric characters
    Population = dplyr::case_when(
      Tract %in% c("Census.Tract.1188..Cuyahoga.County..Ohio",
                   "Census.Tract.1413..Cuyahoga.County..Ohio",
                   "Census.Tract.1871.05..Cuyahoga.County..Ohio",
                   "Census.Tract.1871.06..Cuyahoga.County..Ohio",
                   "Census.Tract.1959..Cuyahoga.County..Ohio",
                   "Census.Tract.3102..Geauga.County..Ohio",
                   "Census.Tract.3106..Geauga.County..Ohio",
                   "Census.Tract.3108..Geauga.County..Ohio",
                   "Census.Tract.3109..Geauga.County..Ohio",
                   "Census.Tract.3110..Geauga.County..Ohio",
                   "Census.Tract.3113..Geauga.County..Ohio",
                   "Census.Tract.3114..Geauga.County..Ohio",
                   "Census.Tract.3116..Geauga.County..Ohio",
                   "Census.Tract.3117..Geauga.County..Ohio",
                   "Census.Tract.3118..Geauga.County..Ohio",
                   "Census.Tract.3121..Geauga.County..Ohio",
                   "Census.Tract.3122.02..Geauga.County..Ohio",
                   "Census.Tract.3123..Geauga.County..Ohio",
                   "Census.Tract.3124..Geauga.County..Ohio",
                   "Census.Tract.2064..Lake.County..Ohio",
                   "Census.Tract.9305..Trumbull.County..Ohio"
      ) & Race == "Population" ~ stringr::str_sub(Population, 1, 5),
      .default = Population
    ),
    Population = stringr::str_replace_all(Population, "\\,", ""),
    Population = as.numeric(Population),
    county_name = stringr::str_sub(Tract, 16, -6),
    county_name = stringr::str_replace_all(county_name, c("[0-9]" = "", "\\." = " ")),
    county_name = trimws(county_name, which = "both", whitespace = "[ \\t\\r\\n\\h]"),
    tract = stringr::str_sub(Tract, 14, 20),
    tract = stringr::str_replace_all(tract, "[A-Za-z]", ""),
    # repeated to remove sets of double periods
    tract = stringr::str_replace_all(tract, "\\.$|\\.\\.$", ""),
    # tract = stringr::str_replace_all(tract, "\\.$", ""),
    tract4 = stringr::str_pad(stringr::str_extract(tract, "^([^.]+)"),
                              width = 4,
                              side = "left",
                              pad = "0"),
    tract2 = stringr::str_pad(stringr::str_extract(tract, "(?<=\\.)[^.]+$"),
                              width = 2,
                              side = "left",
                              pad = "0"),
    tract2 = ifelse(is.na(tract2),"00",tract2),
    tract_formatted = paste0(tract4, tract2)
  ) %>%
  dplyr::left_join(county_fips_xwalk, dplyr::join_by("county_name" == "county")) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    Geography = paste0("39",fips,tract_formatted)
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(Geography, Race, Population) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = "Race", values_from = "Population") %>%
  # reorder columns
  dplyr::select(Geography, Population, White, Black, Hispanic, Asian, NHPI, AIAN, Other,
                `Two or More Races`)



### Demographic Data (2010) - 113th Congressional Districts ----------------------------------------

census_data_113th <- congress_pop_data_113 %>%
  dplyr::mutate(`Label..Grouping.` = trimws(`Label..Grouping.`, which = "both",
                                            whitespace = "[ \\t\\r\\n\\h]")) %>%
  dplyr::filter(`Label..Grouping.` %in% c(
    "Total:",
    "Hispanic or Latino",
    "White alone",
    "Black or African American alone",
    "American Indian and Alaska Native alone",
    "Asian alone",
    "Native Hawaiian and Other Pacific Islander alone",
    "Some Other Race alone",
    "Two or More Races:"
  )) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(Race = dplyr::case_match(
    `Label..Grouping.`,
    "Total:" ~ "Population",
    "Hispanic or Latino" ~ "Hispanic",
    "White alone" ~ "White",
    "Black or African American alone" ~ "Black",
    "American Indian and Alaska Native alone" ~ "AIAN",
    "Asian alone" ~ "Asian",
    "Native Hawaiian and Other Pacific Islander alone" ~ "NHPI",
    "Some Other Race alone" ~ "Other",
    "Two or More Races:" ~ "Two or More Races"
  ), .before = 1) %>%
  dplyr::select(-`Label..Grouping.`) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(2:17, names_to = "District", values_to = "Population") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    Population = stringr::str_replace_all(Population, "\\,", ""),
    Population = as.numeric(Population),
    District = stringr::str_sub(District, 24, 25),
    District = stringr::str_replace_all(District, "\\.", ""),
    District = factor(District, levels = c(1:16))
  ) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = "Race", values_from = "Population") %>%
  # reorder columns
  dplyr::select(District, Population, White, Black, Hispanic, Asian, NHPI, AIAN, Other,
                `Two or More Races`) %>%
  # add additional calculations
  dplyr::mutate(
    `White %` = 100 * White / Population,
    `Black %` = 100 * Black / Population,
    `Hispanic %` = 100 * Hispanic / Population,
    `Asian %` = 100 * Asian / Population,
    `NHPI %` = 100 * NHPI / Population,
    `AIAN %` = 100 * AIAN / Population,
    `Other %` = 100 * Other / Population,
    `Two or More Races %` = 100 * `Two or More Races` / Population,
    `Non-White %` = 100 - `White %`,
    `White Minus Non-White %` = `White %` - `Non-White %`,
    `Diversity Index` = 1 - ((`White %` / 100)^2 + (`Black %` / 100)^2 + (`Hispanic %` / 100)^2 +
                               (`Asian %` / 100)^2 + (`NHPI %` / 100)^2 +(`AIAN %` / 100)^2 +
                               (`Other %` / 100)^2) + (`Two or More Races %` / 100)^2,
    `Population Target Ratio` = 100 * Population / (sum(Population, na.rm = TRUE) / 16)
  )

  dplyr::summarise(
```

## Introduction
The United States House of Representatives is composed of 435 voting members, each elected from a single-representative first-past-the-post district. The number of districts a state receives is proportional to its population, with each district within each state and all districts across the country striving to have roughly equal populations.

For a majority of states, the state must split up its territory into two or more congressional districts. District requirements vary by state, but across all states must be contiguous and all districts in the state must have equal populations (of which states differ on acceptable differences). Building off census tracts, an innumerable combination of congressional districts arise even in states like Idaho or Maine, each of which have two congressional districts. Each state sets its own methods for creating district maps; the methods can emphasize certain aspects, such as requirements for majority-minority districts. Overall, however, the main division to emerge in recent decades is between maps drawn by politically-neutral or politically-balanced committees and those drawn by partisan elected officials.

...

Ohio, a state until recently dubbed a bellwether state for presidential elections, has been one of a handful of states to receive heightened scrutiny for its redistricting practices.^["A Bellwether Refresher: The States Most Likely To Mirror National Election Outcome" by Ron Elving, NPR. https://www.npr.org/2016/11/06/500898858/a-bellwether-refresher-the-states-most-likely-to-mirror-national-election-outcom]

...

## Methodology
Congressional district maps for Ohio are procedurally generated, using only United States Census total population counts and geographical information (e.g., tract adjacency). Additional demographic information, namely race and ethnicity data, is intentionally excluded from this study. While using this data is legal - indeed, even required - in some states to ensure majority-minority district requirements are fulfilled, one of my goals is to assess whether the created districts show notable bias against particular groups. Without the inclusion of race and ethnicity, is there potential for an algorithmic approach to district creation to dilute non-white non-Hispanic groups' electoral power? Ohio has only limited ability to test this, with the state being overwhelmingly white, non-Hispanic. Substantial concentrations of other groups, particularly Black, non-Hispanic communities, exist in and around several large cities such as Cleveland, Akron, and Columbus. However, in the case of Ohio, this largely amounts to testing whether and how an algorithm might break up urban areas.

During the 2020 election, Ohio had 16 congressional seats. Leveraging this count as a power of two, my algorithm splits an area into two areas with equal populations; recursively executing this process results in 16 districts. The following steps are conducted to split a geography in two:

1. Filter out the six unpopulated census tracts containing only water in Lake Erie. Filter out enclave census tract(s) from the data and merge their populations with the surrounding census tract. This ensures the enclave tract will always be in the same district as the surrounding tract.
2. Randomly select two census tracts ($tract_{1}$ and $tract_{2}$) from the population of tracts.
3. For each census tract in the population, calculate the distance (the minimum number of tracts needed to cross to reach one tract from another) to both random tracts $tract_{1}$ and $tract_{2}$ ($dist_{1}$ and $dist_{2}$).
4. Calculate the relative distance from each census tract to $tract_{1}$ and $tract_{2}$, defined as the difference of distances $dist_{r} = dist_{2} - dist_{1}$.
5. Identify the most extreme relative distances (i.e., the highest and lowest $dist_{r}$): $d_{-}$ and $d_{+}$. Identify all census tracts with these respective values, where $\mathbf A$ is the group of tracts with $dist_{r} == d_{-}$ and $\mathbf B$ is the group where $dist_{r} == d_{+}$. For each group, assess whether the group contains only one tract. If the group contains multiple tracts, assess whether all tracts are contiguous. If the tracts are discontiguous, determine the group with the largest count of contiguous tracts and remove all other tracts from the group.
6. Calculate the populations of $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$. Additionally, calculate the target population for the districts, defined as $\frac{\sum x}{2} - \hat{x}$, where $x$ is the census tract population and $\hat{x}$ is the median tract population. As the cutoff population is calculated after a census tract's population is added, this factors in the addition of the population causing the district to exceed the population cutoff value. The population target will vary depending on the composition of the tract population. In the inital step of dividing Ohio into two districts, the population target is 49.968%.
7. Expand $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ by incorporating adjacent census tracts with values of $d_{-}+1$ and $d_{+}-1$, respectively.
8. Repeat this process, recalculating adjacent census tracts and the populations of $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ after each step, until the population of either $\mathbf A$ or $\mathbf B$ surpasses the target population.
9. Assign all census tracts in the population not assigned to $\mathbf A$ or $\mathbf B$ to the set with the smaller population.
10. Calculate continuity of $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$. Reassign any tracts disconnected from the contiguous group with the largest count of districts to the other set $\mathbf B$ or $\mathbf A$.
11. While the populations of $\mathbf A$ or $\mathbf B$ are less than the population goal, reassign census tracts from the smaller district $\mathbf X$ that border the largest district $\mathbf Y$ starting with those with the largest percentage of adjacent tracts belonging to $\mathbf Y$.
11. Iterate through the previous two steps until both $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ are contiguous and have populations above the population target.
12. Reincorporate enclave census tracts by assigning them the district of the surrounding tract.

The result will be two districts with roughly even populations between $\frac{\sum x}{2} - \hat{x}$ and $\frac{\sum x}{2} + \hat{x}$. The process is repeated using these new districts as the starting populations of subsequent splits until a total of 16 districts are created. The process through to this result is referred to as a "run" and the resulting assignment of all census tracts into one of 16 districts is called a "map."

Below are visualization of key steps in the above process.

```{r map_row1, echo=FALSE, out.width="45%", out.height="20%", fig.cap=" ", fig.show='hold', fig.align='center'}

knitr::include_graphics(c("methodology_map_step1_edited.png", "methodology_map_step2_3.png"))

```

```{r map_row2, echo=FALSE, out.width="45%", out.height="20%", fig.cap=" ", fig.show='hold', fig.align='center'}

knitr::include_graphics(c("methodology_map_step3.png","methodology_map_step4.png"))

```


To test whether an algorithm randomly constructing congressional districts within the typical confines - contiguous, equal populations - I use Ohio as an example. Using the post-2010 United States Census redistricting, population data from 2010 is used in conjunction with Ohio's 2020 election results, which use districts based on the 2010 Census. Results will be compared across four aspects, with multiple specific metrics compared within these aspects:

1. **Partisanship**: Assessing district competitiveness and how many seats each map produces for each candidate compared to the 113th Congress's actual seat allocation and the number of votes each party received state-wide.
2. **Population**: Verifying whether the maps fulfill equal population requirements and comparing to the 113th Congress's district populations.
3. **Race/Ethnicity**: Assessing racial and ethnic group distribution across the districts and compared to districts for the 113th Congress's racial and ethnic spread.
4. **District Compactness**: Utilizing several operationalisations of district compactness.

## Findings
### Partisanship
```{r partisanship, include=FALSE}

## Statistical Tests -------------------------------------------------------------------------------
winners_by_run <- data.frame()

for(a in 1:length(partisanship_data)){
  
  tmp <- partisanship_data[[a]] %>%
    dplyr::group_by(Winner) %>%
    dplyr::tally(name = "Won") %>%
    dplyr::ungroup() %>%
    tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = "Winner", values_from = "Won") %>%
    dplyr::mutate(Run = a, .before = 1)
  
  winners_by_run <- rbind(winners_by_run, tmp)
  
}

winners_by_run_long <- winners_by_run %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(2:3, names_to = "Party", values_to = "Seats") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(Party = factor(Party, levels = c("Democrat", "Republican")))

winners_dem <- winners_by_run %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(2:3, names_to = "Winner", values_to = "Value") %>%
  dplyr::filter(Winner == "Democrat")

winners_rep <- winners_by_run %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(2:3, names_to = "Winner", values_to = "Value") %>%
  dplyr::filter(Winner == "Republican")

# comparing against PR 2020 congressional results
t.test(x = winners_dem$Value, alternative = "two.sided",
       mu = expected_pr_results$`Seat Allocation`[expected_pr_results$Party=="Democrat"],
       conf.level = 0.95)

t.test(x = winners_rep$Value, alternative = "two.sided",
       mu = expected_pr_results$`Seat Allocation`[expected_pr_results$Party=="Republican"],
       conf.level = 0.95)

# comparing against actual 2020 congressional results
t.test(x = winners_dem$Value, alternative = "two.sided",
       mu = 4,
       conf.level = 0.95)

t.test(x = winners_rep$Value, alternative = "two.sided",
       mu = 12,
       conf.level = 0.95)


### win margin by run ----------------------------------------------------------------------

win_margins <- list()

for(a in 1:length(partisanship_data)){

  tmp <- partisanship_data[[a]]

  win_margins[[a]] <- c(tmp$Victory_Margin_2Party)

}

# absolute win margin - does not take into account which party won
win_margin_absolute_mean <- lapply(lapply(win_margins, abs), mean) %>% unlist()
win_margin_absolute_median <- lapply(lapply(win_margins, abs), median) %>% unlist()
win_margin_absolute_min <- lapply(lapply(win_margins, abs), min) %>% unlist()
win_margin_absolute_max <- lapply(lapply(win_margins, abs), max) %>% unlist()

# relative win margin - does take into account which party won
win_margin_relative_mean <- lapply(win_margins, mean) %>% unlist()
win_margin_relative_median <- lapply(win_margins, median) %>% unlist()
win_margin_relative_min <- lapply(win_margins, min) %>% unlist()
win_margin_relative_max <- lapply(win_margins, max) %>% unlist()

```
As a comparison for what a partisanly "fair" district map of Ohio should look like, two allocations of seats using the 2020 vote are calculated: one using votes for the presidential race and one using the party of votes for the congressional race. Both results are compiled at the state level and seats are assigned using proportional representation, assigned using the Sainte-Laguë method. These results apply Ohioans' votes proportionally, such that the ratio of votes for each party matches the ratio of congressional seats allotted to that party. Between these two methods, each has distinct strengths and weaknesses. The presidential race is consistent across the entire state (and, excluding third-party ballot access, the entire country), removing possible impacts of candidate-specific differences seen when comparing votes for different congressional candidates. Using congressional election results, however, is measuring the results of the actual elections the model is attempting to assess; individuals may vote differently for a presidential candidate - a heavily nationalized race - versus a congressional candidate - historically more tied to local issues. As politics have become increasingly nationalized over the last several decades, however, the impact of split-ticket voters has lessened.

Despite their theoretical differences, both calculations result in the same allocation of seats based on the 2020 results: `r sum(presidential_results_sainte_lague == 1)` seats for Republicans and `r sum(presidential_results_sainte_lague == 2)` seats for Democrats. Actual results saw 12 Republicans and 4 Democrats winning seats for the 117th United States Congress.

Based on `r nrow(winners_by_run)` procedurally generated congressional maps of Ohio's 16 seats using 2010 Census data, the average number of seats won by Republicans was `r round(median(winners_by_run$Republican))` and won by Democrats was `r round(median(winners_by_run$Democrat))`. Table 1 shows the frequency of number of seats won by party.

```{r winner_frequency_plot, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

ggplot2::ggplot() +

  ) +

                     breaks = seq(0, 16, 2)) +

  ggplot2::theme_light()

```

The random algorithm on average produced a seat distribution of 11 Republican to 5 Democrat seats, which is closer to the expected proportional representation than the actual results.

#### District Competitiveness
**Absolute Win Margin.** The absolute win margin is calculated as the absolute value of the difference in the two-party percentage, such that the winner being a Democrat or Republican is not factored into the value. This excludes any third-party or write-in votes. $w_{abs} = |\frac{votes_{d}}{votes_{d} + votes_{r}} - \frac{votes_{r}}{votes_{d} + votes_{r}}|$, where $w_{abs}$ is the absolute win margin of a district and $votes_{d}$ and $votes_{r}$ are the count of votes for the Democratic and Republican candidates, respectively. This can be simplified to $w_{abs} = \frac{|votes_{d} - votes_{r}|}{votes_{d} + votes_{r}}$. The values are confined between 0 and 100, with 0 representing an exactly even split of votes between the Democrat and Republican and 100 representing one of the candidate receiving every vote while the other candidate receives none. This value is akin to a Cook Political Score value or other similar district partisan measurements, absent the direction of the political lean.

Table XX shows summary statistics calculated for each run, with the 113th Congress's results shown in red. For mean and median results, a higher value indicates the average district within that map of 16 districts is more partisan. For minimum results, a higher value indicates the least partisan district (i.e., the most competitive district) is more partisan (less competitive); for maximum results, a lower value indicates the most partisan district (i.e., the "safest" district) is less partisan (more competitive).

Overall, lower values indicate higher electoral competitiveness.

```{r district_competitiveness_absolute, echo=FALSE}

win_margin_absolute_df <- data.frame(
  run = c(1:length(win_margin_absolute_median)),
  Mean = win_margin_absolute_mean,
  Median = win_margin_absolute_median,
  Minimum = win_margin_absolute_min,
  Maximum = win_margin_absolute_max,
  # group color = 1 is for runs, color = 2 is for 113th congress actuals
  Group = "Runs"
  ) %>%
  tibble::add_row(
    run = NA,
    Mean = 100 * mean(results$`Absolute Win Margin`, na.rm = TRUE),
    Median = 100 * median(results$`Absolute Win Margin`, na.rm = TRUE),
    Minimum = 100 * min(results$`Absolute Win Margin`, na.rm = TRUE),
    Maximum = 100 * max(results$`Absolute Win Margin`, na.rm = TRUE),
    Group = "Actual"
  ) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(2:5, names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    variable = factor(
      variable,
      levels = c("Mean", "Median", "Minimum", "Maximum")
      ),
    Group = factor(
      Group,
      levels = c("Runs", "Actual")
    ))

ggplot2::ggplot() +
  ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm(data = win_margin_absolute_df,
                            ggplot2::aes(x = variable, y = value, color = Group)) +
  ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = c("black", "red", "blue", "black")) +
  # ggplot2::geom_hline(ggplot2::aes(yintercept = ohio_diversity_index, color = "Ohio Avg."), linetype = "dotdash")  +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "Absolute Win Margin",
    subtitle = "Run Averages versus 113th Congress",
    x = "Summary Value by Run",
    y = "Points of Absolute Win Margin",
    caption = "Sources: Redistricting Data Hub (RDH), 2020 results"
    ) +
  ggplot2::ylim(c(0, 65)) +
  ggplot2::theme_light()

```

Across all the procedurally generated maps, all show average (both calculated as mean and median) districts as more competitive than the 113th district results. A majority of districts also had more competitive most-competitive districts and all but one map had more competitive least-competitive districts.

**Relative Win Margin.** The relative win margin is calculated as the directed value of the difference in the two-party percentage, such that positive or negative values indicate a Democrat or Republican won more votes, respectively. Once again, this excludes any third-party or write-in votes. $w_{rel} = \frac{votes_{d}}{votes_{d} + votes_{r}} - \frac{votes_{r}}{votes_{d} + votes_{r}}$, which simplifies to $w_{rel} = \frac{votes_{d} - votes_{r}}{votes_{d} + votes_{r}}$, where $w_{rel}$ is the absolute win margin of a district and $votes_{d}$ and $votes_{r}$ are the count of votes for the Democratic and Republican candidates, respectively. The values are confined between -100 and 100, with -100 indicating a Republican won all the two-party votes, a 0 indicating the Democrat and Republican won equal number of votes, and a 100 indicating a Democrat won all the two-party votes. The absolute value of this metric is the absolute win margin $w_{abs}$. This value is akin to a Cook Political Score value or other similar district partisan measurements.

```{r district_competitiveness_relative, echo=FALSE}

      ),
    Group = factor(
      Group,
      levels = c("Runs", "Actual")
    ))

ggplot2::ggplot() +

  ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = c("black", "red", "blue", "black")) +
  # ggplot2::geom_hline(ggplot2::aes(yintercept = ohio_diversity_index, color = "Ohio Avg."), linetype = "dotdash")  +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "Relative Win Margin",
    subtitle = "Run Averages versus 113th Congress",
```

```{r pop_numbers, include=FALSE}

#### pull metrics by run ----------------------------------------------------------------------

population_target_ratio_values_median <- lapply(population_target_ratio_values, median) %>% unlist()
population_target_ratio_values_min <- lapply(population_target_ratio_values, min) %>% unlist()
population_target_ratio_values_max <- lapply(population_target_ratio_values, max) %>% unlist()

# pretty versions of numbers for use in text

# district target population (rounded)
target_pop <- prettyNum(round(sum(population_data$Population)/16), big.mark = ",")

# district population legal spread in 2010
target_pop_spread <- prettyNum(round(0.1*sum(population_data$Population)/16), big.mark = ",")
  

# 113th Congress population extremes - Census
congress113_min_value <- prettyNum(round(min(census_data_113th$Population)), big.mark = ",")
congress113_max_value <- prettyNum(round(max(census_data_113th$Population)), big.mark = ",")

congress113_min_perc <- round(min(census_data_113th$`Population Target Ratio`),2)
congress113_max_perc <- round(max(census_data_113th$`Population Target Ratio`),2)

# number of generated maps
num_gen_maps <- length(population_target_ratio_values_median)

# generated maps population extremes - Census
gen_maps_min_value_min <- prettyNum(round((min(population_target_ratio_values_min)/100)*(sum(population_data$Population)/16)), big.mark = ",")
gen_maps_max_value_max <- prettyNum(round((max(population_target_ratio_values_max)/100)*sum(population_data$Population)/16), big.mark = ",")

gen_maps_min_perc_min <- round(min(population_target_ratio_values_min),2)
gen_maps_max_perc_max <- round(max(population_target_ratio_values_max),2)

gen_maps_min_value_median <- prettyNum(round((median(population_target_ratio_values_min)/100)*(sum(population_data$Population)/16)), big.mark = ",")
gen_maps_max_value_median <- prettyNum(round((median(population_target_ratio_values_max)/100)*sum(population_data$Population)/16), big.mark = ",")

gen_maps_min_perc_median <- round(median(population_target_ratio_values_min),2)
gen_maps_max_perc_median <- round(median(population_target_ratio_values_max),2)

```
Congressional districts within each state are required to have equal populations, though the degree of their margin of error varies by state. Ultimately, districts will have small deviations above or below the target amount due to compiling geographic units of various populations. Ohio's Constitution, as updated in 2021, stipulates that "[i]n no event shall any district contain a population of less than ninety-five per cent nor more than one hundred five per cent of the applicable ratio of representation" (Article XI, Section 3(B)(1)).^[Ohio Constitution Article XI, Section 3: https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-constitution/section-11.3] This allows districts to have a population range of 10% of the target district population as measured by the decennial census, which based on the 2010 Census would be `r target_pop_spread` individuals.

For Ohio's redrawing following the 2010 Census, each district was expected to have approximately `r target_pop` individuals across its now 16 congressional districts. Using the same 2010 Census data, Ohio's districts in the 113th Congress ranged from `r congress113_min_value` individuals (`r congress113_min_perc`% of the target population) to `r congress113_max_value` individuals (`r congress113_max_perc`%).

States are forbidden from use race or ethnicity to politically disadvantage one or more particular groups. However, several states require the creation of one or more majority-minority districts, that is, a district with a larger proportion of Hispanic and non-White individuals than non-Hispanic White individuals. With the strong (though decreasing) correlation between race/ethnicity and voting patterns, separating redistricting based on demographic and partisan characteristics is challenging.

Overall, Ohio's population according to the 2010 Census was `r ohio_white_perc`% White, `r ohio_black_perc`% Black, `r ohio_hispanic_perc`% Hispanic, `r ohio_asian_perc`% Asian, `r ohio_aian_perc`% American Indian or Alaskan Native (AIAN), `r ohio_nhpi_perc`% Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander (NHPI), `r ohio_other_perc`% other race, and `r ohio_twoormore_perc`% individuals identifying as two or more races. (Note Hispanic includes all individuals identifying as Hispanic regardless of racial identification. All race categories are for non-Hispanic individuals.) The proportion of individuals identifying as non-White in Ohio is `r ohio_nonwhite_perc`%.

```{r diversity_index, include=FALSE}
ohio_statewide_diversity_index <- population_data %>%
  dplyr::group_by() %>%
  dplyr::summarise(across(c(White, Black, Hispanic, AIAN, Asian, NHPI, Other, `Two or More Races`), sum, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  dplyr::ungroup() %>%
  t() %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  dplyr::rename(Count = 1) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    Perc = Count / sum(population_data$Population, na.rm = TRUE),
    Perc_Squared = Perc^2
  )
ohio_diversity_index <- 1 - sum(ohio_statewide_diversity_index$Perc_Squared, na.rm = TRUE)
# 0.3258022
  
diversity_index_df <- data.frame(
  run = c(1:length(diversity_index_values_median)),
  Median = diversity_index_values_median,
  Minimum = diversity_index_values_min,
  Maximum = diversity_index_values_max,
  # group color = 1 is for runs, color = 2 is for 113th congress actuals
  Group = "Runs"
  ) %>%
  tibble::add_row(
    run = NA,
    Median = median(census_data_113th$`Diversity Index`, na.rm = TRUE),
    Minimum = min(census_data_113th$`Diversity Index`, na.rm = TRUE),
    Maximum = max(census_data_113th$`Diversity Index`, na.rm = TRUE),
    Group = "Actual"
  ) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(2:4, names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    variable = factor(
      variable,
      levels = c("Median", "Minimum", "Maximum")
      ),
    Group = factor(
      Group,
      levels = c("Runs", "Actual")
    ))

```

The Diversity Index is a commonly used measurement calculating the racial/ethnic diversity within a given area, including use by the United States Census Bureau.^["Racial and Ethnic Diversity in the United States: 2010 Census and 2020 Census", United States Census Bureau. https://www.census.gov/library/visualizations/interactive/racial-and-ethnic-diversity-in-the-united-states-2010-and-2020-census.html] The Diversity Index is defined as $D = 1 - \sum_{}^{} \rho_{i}^{2}$, where $\rho_{i}$ is the proportion of the population belonging to each of the eight race/ethnicity groupings. A higher index score indicates greater diversity.

Table XX shows summary statistics for district diversity indices along with summary statistics for the 113th Congress. Ohio's state-wide Diversity Index, $D_{OH} = 0.326$, is shown as a red dashed line. Points above this line are more racially/ethnically diverse than Ohio overall, while points below this line are less so.

Looking at the minimum and maximum Diversity Index scores by map, lower minimum values and higher maximum values are a potential indication of packing or cracking racial groups. This may be done unintentionally, it may be unavoidable due to the distribution of racial and ethnic groups, or it may be done intentionally in the case of majority-minority districts.

```{r diversity_index_plot, echo=FALSE}
  ggplot2::geom_hline(ggplot2::aes(yintercept = ohio_diversity_index, color = "Ohio Avg."), linetype = "dotdash")  +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "TABLE XX. Diversity Index Summary Values",
    subtitle = "Run Averages versus 113th Congress",
    x = "Summary Value by Run",
    y = "Diversity Index Value",
    caption = "Sources: US Census Bureau, 2010 Census"
    ) +
  ggplot2::theme_light() +
  ggplot2::theme(
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank()
  )
  
```

Another prominent measurement of racial/ethnic distribution is calculating the difference in the proportion of non-Hispanic White individuals versus non-White individuals.

```{r white_minus_nonwhite_perc, include=FALSE}

# White % - Non-White % summary values by map
white_minus_nonwhite_values_mean <- lapply(white_minus_nonwhite_values, mean) %>% unlist()
white_minus_nonwhite_values_median <- lapply(white_minus_nonwhite_values, median) %>% unlist()
white_minus_nonwhite_values_min <- lapply(white_minus_nonwhite_values, min) %>% unlist()
white_minus_nonwhite_values_max <- lapply(white_minus_nonwhite_values, max) %>% unlist()

ohio_statewide_white_percent <- 100 * sum(population_data$White, na.rm = TRUE) /
                                        sum(population_data$Population, na.rm = TRUE)
ohio_statewide_nonwhite_percent <- 100 * (sum(population_data$Population, na.rm = TRUE) -
                                            sum(population_data$White, na.rm = TRUE)) /
                                            sum(population_data$Population, na.rm = TRUE)

ohio_white_minus_nonwhite <- ohio_statewide_white_percent - ohio_statewide_nonwhite_percent
# 62.25475

white_minus_nonwhite_df <- data.frame(
  run = c(1:length(white_minus_nonwhite_values_median)),
  Median = white_minus_nonwhite_values_median,
  Minimum = white_minus_nonwhite_values_min,
  Maximum = white_minus_nonwhite_values_max,
  # group color = 1 is for runs, color = 2 is for 113th congress actuals
  Group = "Runs"
) %>%
  tibble::add_row(
    run = NA,
    Median = median(census_data_113th$`White Minus Non-White %`, na.rm = TRUE),
    Minimum = min(census_data_113th$`White Minus Non-White %`, na.rm = TRUE),
    Maximum = max(census_data_113th$`White Minus Non-White %`, na.rm = TRUE),
    Group = "Actual"
  ) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(2:4, names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    variable = factor(
      variable,
      levels = c("Median", "Minimum", "Maximum")
    ),
    Group = factor(
      Group,
      levels = c("Runs", "Actual")
    ))

ggplot2::ggplot() +
  ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm(data = white_minus_nonwhite_df,
                            ggplot2::aes(x = variable, y = value, color = Group)) +
  ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = c("black", "red", "black")) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(ggplot2::aes(yintercept = ohio_white_minus_nonwhite, color = "Ohio Avg."), linetype = "dotdash")  +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "TABLE XX. White % Minus Non-White % Summary Values",
    subtitle = "Run Averages versus 112th Congress",
    x = "Summary Value by Run",
    y = "Percentage Value",
    caption = "Sources: US Census Bureau, 2010 Census;\nAmerican Community Survey (ACS), 2012\nNote: Ethnicity data not included"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_light()


# beeswarm of all districts - white % minus non-white %
white_minus_nonwhite_all_df <- data.frame(Group = "Runs",
                                          value = unlist(white_minus_nonwhite_values)) %>%
  rbind(data.frame(Group = "Actual",
                   value = c(census_data_113th$`White Minus Non-White %`))) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(Group = factor(Group, levels = c("Runs", "Actual")))

ggplot2::ggplot() +
  ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm(data = white_minus_nonwhite_all_df,
                            ggplot2::aes(x = Group, y = value, color = Group)) +
  ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = c("black", "red", "black")) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(ggplot2::aes(yintercept = ohio_white_minus_nonwhite, color = "Ohio Avg."), linetype = "dotdash") +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "White % Minus Non-White % Summary Values",
    subtitle = "Runs versus 112th Congress",
    x = "Summary Value",
    y = "Percentage Value",
    caption = "Sources: US Census Bureau, 2010 Census;\nAmerican Community Survey (ACS), 2012\nNote: Ethnicity data not included"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_light() +
  ggplot2::theme(
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank()
  )
```

### District Compactness
```{r compactness_general, include=FALSE}

### compare averages ----------------------------------------------------------------------
average_polsby_popper <- c()
average_schwartzberg <- c()
average_reock <- c()

for(l in 1:length(compactness_data)){
  
  tmp <- compactness_data[[l]]
  
  average_polsby_popper <- c(average_polsby_popper,
                             mean(tmp$Compactness.Polsby.Popper, na.rm = TRUE))
  average_schwartzberg <- c(average_polsby_popper,
                            mean(tmp$Compactness.Schwartzberg, na.rm = TRUE))
  average_reock <- c(average_polsby_popper,
                     mean(tmp$Compactness.Reock, na.rm = TRUE))
  
}

# actual scores by congressional session
average_compactness_scores_actual <- compactness_data_actual %>%
  dplyr::group_by(Congressional.Session) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(
    Compactness.Polsby.Popper = mean(Compactness.Polsby.Popper, na.rm = TRUE),
    Compactness.Schwartzberg = mean(Compactness.Schwartzberg, na.rm = TRUE),
    Compactness.Reock = mean(Compactness.Reock, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  dplyr::ungroup()
```
